text: Eger Vaughan Murphree (November 3, 1898 – October 29, 1962) was an American chemist best known for co-inventing the process of fluid catalytic cracking. Born in Bayonne, New Jersey, he moved to Kentucky as a child and graduated from Kentucky University with degrees in chemistry and mathematics in 1920, earning a master's degree in chemistry in 1921. He played college football as a tackle for Kentucky and served as captain of the 1920 Kentucky Wildcats football team. After teaching physics and math and coaching football for one year at Paris High School in Paris, Illinois, Murphree worked several years at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology as a staff assistant and research associate in the Chemical Engineering Department. In 1930, he joined Standard Oil of New Jersey. During the Second World War, he was a member of the committee that organized the Manhattan Project and was recognized as a leader in synthetic toluene, butadiene and hydrocarbon synthesis, fluid catalytic cracking, fluid hydroforming, and fluid coking. He participated in the early Manhattan Project as a member of the S-1 Section, served as head of the centrifuge project (which was later abandoned), and was the overall engineer for the Manhattan Project in June 1942. He described Deputy District Engineer Kenneth Nichols as "more like the industrial engineers I was accustomed to dealing with—stable, conservative, thorough and precise." He was scheduled to be on the Lewis Committee reviewing the project in November 1942 but was ill; he (along with James Conant) opposed the committee’s recommendation to build only a small electromagnetic plant, and a full-size plant was constructed. In the 1950s, he served in the Defense Department on missile scheduling and coordinating the programs of the three military services, a role previously held by Nichols. From 1947 to 1962, he served as Vice President of research and engineering at Standard Oil of New Jersey, the company later known as Exxon. He received the Perkin Medal in 1950 and the Industrial Research Institute (IRI) Medal in 1953. The E. V. Murphree Award in Industrial and Engineering Chemistry, awarded annually by the American Chemical Society, is named in his honor. Murphree died on October 29, 1962, at Overlook Hospital in Summit, New Jersey, from coronary thrombosis. He was inducted into the National Inventors Hall of Fame in 1999.
